messages.author: b2bc3c8f70c34410
messages.subject: Need for speed with PVA
parts:
Hi Folks,
I have an Integrated Population Model (IPM) that I've turned into a Population Viability Analysis (PVA). The IPM is comprised of several submodels including: productivity, multi-state Cormack-Jolly-Seber mark-recapture, count data, and a population model. I can run the IPM in about 1-2 days, but when I project the model into the future (45 scenarios, 50 years) the model becomes intractible (>12 day runtime). So I'm looking for strategies on speeding up the model/simulations, especially if there are any obvious bottlenecks. 

Here are a few things I've already tried to speed computation
(A) I've parallelized the chains for running on an HPC. 
(B) I've added non-centered random effects - this sped convergence greatly
(C) I tried to add HMC on non-discrete portions of the model- this returns an error when I add buildDerivs=TRUE, maybe because of the dcat distribution with stochastic indexing (discussed here).

Here are a few things I'm thinking about trying:
(1) Can I add posterior draws from the IPM to the PVA so parameters are already converged and just simulate from those for the PVA part? This would be easiest to implement and fastest. Is this possible? 
(2) Reparameterize around computational bottlenecks to increase speed.
(3) Vectorize submodels- For example maybe vectorizing across individuals in the mark-recapture model. 
(4) Add HMC by modifying the dcat distribution in the mark-recapture model. (See discussion) or by some other way. Maybe use the nimble ecology package for this?
(5) Use nimble functions to speed computation- if so, where would this be most effective?
(6) Use moment matching of estimates from the IPM to simulate from the estimated parameters

I'd like to avoid (6) if possible. I also have no intention of marginalizing out discrete states or using an m-array model because I have individual attributes that affect survival and recruitment. Any other suggestions are welcome.

Here's the full IPM/PVA code. 
Here's the data.
Here's the IPM code for a simplified example without future projections.
This would be difficult to run by others because it relies on initial values from earlier model runs (large file) so chains don't break. Apologies for not having a fully reproducible example. 

Maybe this would be a good opportunity to discuss strategies to speed up models and simulations in general. Thanks in advance.

Cheers,
Brian

messages.subject: Re: Need for speed with PVA
parts:
Brian, a quick note about your (1) Can I add posterior draws from the IPM to the PVA so parameters are already converged and just simulate from those for the PVA part? This would be easiest to implement and fastest. Is this possible? 

The "prior_samples" sampler was added to the MCMC a few releases ago, which should accomplish what you want - using posterior draws (stored in a numeric vector or array) as the prior for a model parameter.  I'll copy the documentation for it below, but let me know if you have questions or problems with it.

Your other suggestions are all viable as well, in particular the vectorization, and using nimbleFunctions to move around how/where computation takes place.

Cheers,
Daniel

#' @section prior_samples sampler:
#'
#' The prior_samples sampler uses a provided set of numeric values (\code{samples}) to define the prior distribution of one or more model nodes.  One every MCMC iteration, the prior_samples sampler takes value(s) from the numeric values provided, and stores these value(s) into the target model node(s).  This allows one to define the prior distribution of model parameters empirically, using a set of numeric \code{samples}, presumably obtained previously using MCMC.  The \code{target} node may be either a single scalar node (scalar case), or a collection of model nodes.
#'
#' The prior_samples sampler provides two options for selection of the value to use on each MCMC iteration.  The default behaviour is to take sequential values from the \code{samples} vector (scalar case), or in the case of multiple dimensions, sequential rows of the \code{samples} matrix are used.  The alternative behaviour, by setting the control argument \code{randomDraws = TRUE}, will instead use random draws from the \code{samples} vector (scalar case), or randomly selected rows of the \code{samples} matrix in the multidimensional case.
#'
#' If the default of sequential selection of values is used, and the number of MCMC iterations exceeds the length of the \code{samples} vector (scalar case) or the number of rows of the \code{samples} matrix, then \code{samples} will be recycled as necessary for the number of MCMC iterations.  A message to this effect is also printed at the beginning of the MCMC chain.
#'
#' Logically, prior_samples samplers might want to operate first, in advance of other samplers, on every MCMC iteration.  By default, at the time of MCMC building, all prior_samples samplers are re-ordered to appear first in the list of MCMC samplers.  This behaviour can be subverted, however, by setting nimbleOptions(MCMCorderPriorSamplesSamplersFirst = FALSE).
#'
#' The prior_samples sampler can be assigned to non-stochastic model nodes (nodes which are not assigned a prior distribution in the model). In fact, it is recommended that nodes being assigned a prior_samples are not provided with a prior distribution in the model, and rather, that these nodes only appear on the right-hand-side of model declaration lines.  In such case that a prior_samples sampler is assigned to a nodes with a prior distribution, the prior distribution will be overridden by the sample values provided to the sampler; however, the node will still be a stochastic node for other purposes, and will contribute to the model joint-density (using the sample values provided relative to the prior distribution), will have an MCMC sampler assigned to it by default, and also may introduce potential for confusion.  In this case, a message is issued at the time of MCMC building.
#'
#' The prior_samples sampler accepts the following control list elements:
#' \itemize{
#' \item \code{samples}. A numeric vector or matrix.  When the \code{target} node is a single scalar-valued node, \code{samples} should be a numeric vector.  When the \code{target} node specifies d > 2 model dimensions, \code{samples} should be a matrix containing d columns.  The \code{samples} control argument is required.
#' \item \code{randomDraws}. A logical argument, specifying whether to use a random draw from \code{samples} on each iteration.  If \code{samples} is a matrix, then a randomly-selected row of the \code{samples} matrix is used.  When \code{FALSE}, sequential values (or sequential matrix rows) are used (default = \code{FALSE}).
#' }

messages.author: d78486bfff620d81
messages.subject: Re: Need for speed with PVA
parts:
Hi Brian, I haven't fully absorbed what you're doing here and haven't looked in detail at your code, but one reaction is as follows.

If the projection part of the model doesn't involve any data (i.e., it is pure posterior simulation given the parameters fitted in the IPM part of the model), then a good strategy would be to fit the IPM part of the model to get samples from the posterior of the IPM parameters and then run the projection for each posterior sample. This could be done in parallel in R without using nimble, or you could use nimbleFunctions to do the projection (this could also be done in parallel, so long as you build the model and compile it any nimbleFunctions separately in each parallel worker). So the second stage would not actually be running an MCMC because you wouldn't be conditioning directly on any data. 

It sounds like you may already have satisfactory mixing in not-too-long for the IPM part of the model, so you may be in a good position to not have to worry further about MCMC mixing, but simply deal with the projection part by "brute force".

Daniel's suggestion for the `prior_samples` sampler would be useful if you did actually have data that were directly part of the projection model.

-chris

parts:
Thanks Daniel,
 I'm struggling a bit with implementing this, even after reading through much of the manuals, and apologies because I'm not well versed in customizing samplers. 

For example, I have a set of nodes in the IPM with priors as 
for (j in 1:3){ sds[j] ~ dexp(1) } # I comment out the prior in the PVA as recommended by the manual

I can do this:
# grepl() finds the node names
subs <- grepl('sds', colnames(post)) # 'post' are my posterior iterations as rows and nodes (sds[1:3]) as columns.
sds.p <- post[ ,subs] # subset to a matrix containing only sds
confhmc$addSampler(target = colnames(sds.p), type = 'prior_samples', samples = sds.p)

When I do this it returns four samplers in the list as
confhmc$getSamplers('sds')
[[1]] 
RW sampler: sds[1] 
[[2]]
prior_samples sampler: sds[1], sds[2], sds[3] samples: custom array'
... 2 more RW samplers

So it retains the former RW samplers. 
(1) Do I need to use confhmc$removeSampler('sds') to remove the RW sampler
(2) Do I need to input these as a list off 3 vectors? For example, 
sds.l <-list( 'sds[1]' = sds.p[, 1], 'sds[2]' = sds.p[, 2], 'sds[3]' = sds.p[, 3] )
confhmc$addSampler(target = colnames(sds.p), type = 'prior_samples', samples = sds.l)

I have some larger 4 dimensional matrices that I'll try to enter as a matrix (as in the help file for >2 dims), but I need to figure out the simpler versions before moving on to that. Maybe an example using a matrix would be helpful as well though.  

Thanks for any advice you can provide and I'm sure others may find this helpful. Also, this is a great solution that will save me lots of time and I really appreciate the added functionality by the nimble team. 
Brian
